headline: Promise check: Shield Texans from rising gas utility bills

headline: Ask Texans to name the state's biggest problem, and the answer depends on their party.
body:
In the October UT/Texas Politics Project poll, Democrats put political corruption and leadership first (30%), then higher prices (18%) and the economy (8%).

Republicans named prices first (22%), then immigration (14%) and the economy (12%). Only 3% picked corruption.

Independents also put prices first (27%), followed by corruption (15%), jobs and unemployment (11%) and data centers (8%).

Keep in mind: the question asks which problem matters most, not which policies people want. Party groups include people who lean toward a party, and "independents" are only those with no lean. Subgroups have larger margins of error than the full poll of 1,200 registered voters (Sep 25 to Oct 5, 2026).

headline: Texas voters picked a Democratic lieutenant governor. Republicans still hold 19 of 31 Senate seats.
body:
Here's why: most of the job's power isn't in the Texas Constitution. The Constitution gives it a few duties: presiding over the Senate and stepping in as governor when needed. The bigger levers (naming committee chairs, sending bills to committees and deciding which bills reach the floor) come from Senate rules.

Senators adopt those rules at the start of each session, and a simple majority (16 votes) can change them. Republicans have 19. KPRC reports the Senate GOP caucus has discussed it. No rules have been changed yet.

What's next: bill pre-filing opens Monday, Nov. 9, and the session starts Jan. 12, 2027.

Why it matters: whoever runs the Senate's agenda shapes which bills on taxes, schools and electricity get a vote.

How much power should the Senate's presiding officer have, no matter which party holds the job?

headline: Will every Texas household get $1,500? Not automatically. Here's what it would take.
body:
Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a one-time $1,500 payment to every Texas household, which she calls a "corruption tax refund." Her campaign puts the cost at about $17 billion, paid from the state's Rainy Day Fund (the Economic Stabilization Fund), which she says holds about $27 billion. About $10 billion would stay in reserve.

A governor can't send the checks alone. Using the fund this way takes a two-thirds vote in both the Texas House and the Texas Senate, where Republicans hold the majority. The Legislature convenes Jan. 12, 2027, and Hinojosa says she'll make it an emergency item. Who qualifies, how to apply and when checks would arrive haven't been decided.

Why it matters: it's money for families, and it's also the state's main savings account.

headline: Can a new governor fire Texas's education chief on day one? The law makes it more complicated.
body:
On election night, Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa said: "On day one, I will fire Mike Morath," the Texas Education Agency commissioner. Her team says it is "actively interviewing" replacements, and she wants an educator in the job.

Here's the catch. Morath's term ends Jan. 10, nine days before Hinojosa is sworn in on Jan. 19. Removing a commissioner before the term ends needs Senate approval. And whoever she picks needs a two-thirds vote of the Texas Senate, where Republicans still hold the majority.

Why it matters: the commissioner oversees A-F school ratings and state takeovers of struggling districts. Seven districts are under takeover now, including Houston and Fort Worth ISD.

headline: Texas has a new governor and lieutenant governor on the way. So who actually holds the power now?
body:
What happened: Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Gov. Greg Abbott, CBS News projects, and Democrat Vikki Goodwin defeated Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, who conceded.

Who decides: The Legislature still writes the laws and the state budget. Republicans keep a majority in the Texas Senate. The Texas House is not called yet: Democrats need 14 flips, and early Wednesday they had 3 and led in about a dozen more. A governor can veto bills, and overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers. Much of the lieutenant governor's power comes from Senate rules that senators vote on each session.

What's next: Bill filing opens Nov. 9. The new leaders take office in January, and the Legislature convenes Jan. 12.

Why it matters: who controls each chamber shapes what happens with property taxes, schools and the budget in 2027.
